<!-- docs/hidden-messages.md -->
## Hidden messages
# Hidden messages
A Typographics Art work can carry a message that only the holder of a key can read. The work itself is not changed: it contains exactly its public text, nothing invisible, no extra characters. The message lives only in the key.
## How it works
It is a book cipher over the work's public text.
1. **The public text** is taken the way a machine reads the work: whitespace normalised, invisible format characters (soft hyphens, direction marks) removed, split into grapheme clusters (`canonicalText` in `src/secret.js`). The same text comes out of the HTML, the SVG and the PDF (read with MuPDF). 2. **Hiding:** for every character of the secret, all its occurrences in the public text are collected and one is chosen at random (Web Crypto, without modulo bias). The key is the list of chosen positions. 3. **Fingerprint:** the key starts with the first 8 bytes of the SHA-256 of the public text. Revealing with another work, or with a changed text, is detected and refused instead of producing garbage. 4. **Revealing:** the characters at the listed positions, joined, are the secret.
## The key
`tg1.` followed by base64url of: 8 bytes text fingerprint, then the positions as variable-length integers (about 3 bytes per character for texts of up to two million characters). The key grows by about 4 characters per character of the secret on top of a short header: measured on a 47 000-character text, 26 characters of secret gave a key of 106 characters; a 30-character secret gives about 120 to 140.
## Use
```sh node cli/tg-secret.mjs hide work.pdf --secret "Meet at the harbour, 6 pm." # prints the key node cli/tg-secret.mjs reveal work.pdf --key tg1.… # prints the message ```
The key is the secret, so it is better not to put it on the command line, where it shows up in the process list and in the shell history: `reveal` also takes it from a file (`--key-file key.txt`), from standard input (`--key-stdin`) or from the environment variable `TG_SECRET_KEY`.
The CLI reads PDF (via MuPDF), SVG, HTML and plain text. In the [web generator](https://typographics-art.org/app), the panel *Hidden message* does the same for the current work. In code: `hideSecret(publicText, secret)` and `revealSecret(publicText, key)` from `src/index.js`.
## What it protects, and what it does not
- **The work reveals nothing.** Without the key it is an ordinary work; there is no hidden layer to find, because there is none. - **The key is the secret.** Whoever has the key and the work can read the message. Share the key over another channel and keep it like a password. - **Random positions:** the same secret gives a different key every time, and repeated letters of the secret point to different places, so the key does not show which letters repeat. - **Not a replacement for encryption** where the message must stay secret even from someone who may get the key: then encrypt the message first and hide the ciphertext's characters, or use proper encryption.
## Limits
- A character that does not occur in the public text cannot be hidden; the tool names the missing characters. Longer texts contain more characters; digits and rare symbols may be absent from short ones. - The key fits exactly one text. Re-setting the same text into a new picture keeps the key valid (the text is the same); changing even one character of the text makes it invalid. - One PDF quirk: after a character drawn from a fallback font (for example "->"), MuPDF may read a following space as missing; such a work's PDF text then differs from its source and the key made from the source does not fit the PDF (see `docs/ai-readability.md`).
## Honesty
This does not touch the [rules of the technique](https://typographics-art.org/docs/technique.md): the work contains its declared text and nothing else. Tiny or invisible text must never be used to hide anything inside a work.
---
<!-- docs/passwords-and-keys.md -->
## Passwords, keys and seeds
# Passwords, keys and seeds: how it works here, and what we do not promise
This page is for people who want to know whether they can trust the way Typographics Art protects data, without reading the cryptography papers. It explains the design in plain words, gives the reasons, and says plainly what is **not** covered. Everything is open source; every number below was measured or is marked as an estimate or a citation, and the last section shows how to check it yourself. The technical documents behind it are [encrypted-data.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/encrypted-data.md), [key-management.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/key-management.md) and [cipher-review.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/cipher-review.md). A German version of this page: [passwords-and-keys.de.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/passwords-and-keys.de.md).
## 1. In one minute
- **The lock is strong.** Sealed data uses AES-256-GCM, a standard cipher that your browser or Node provides. We did not invent a cipher, and we looked at the alternatives (section 7): none is worth the risk of adding code. - **A password is the weak point of every lock like this, so a password never stands alone.** For anything public or permanent, the real protection is a long random secret that nobody types. A password can only be an *additional* factor mixed with it. The tools refuse to publish a record that is protected by a password only. - **You hold the key; we cannot recover it.** The page does its work in your browser and does not send your data, key, seed or password anywhere (the site loads nothing from third parties, and the browser enforces that with a content security policy). That also means: if you lose the key, the data is gone, and nobody can help you. - **It is not independently audited.** The cipher is standard; the code around it (formats, binding, key handling) was written for this project, tested, and reviewed by automated tools, but no outside cryptographer has reviewed it. If losing or leaking the data would really hurt, get a review first.
## 2. The secrets, and what each one is for
| Secret | What it is | Typed by a person? | Used for | |---|---|---|---| | **Random key** (`tgx1.…`, `tgx2.…`) | 256 random bits, shown as about 60 characters | No: copy and paste, or a file | Opens one sealed record. This is the default protection. | | **Seed** (12, 18 or 24 recovery words, or hex) | The one backup from which a **master key** and one **key per record** are derived | Words are written down and typed rarely | Opens everything that was sealed from it; a single record key can be given away without exposing the rest. | | **Password / passphrase** | Something a person remembers | Yes | Only as an *extra* factor (never alone for public data). | | **Share** (`tgsh1.…`) | One piece of a key split in several pieces | No | A key that needs several pieces from different hands (any k of n). | | **Passkey** (WebAuthn, the phone or a security key) | A hardware-bound secret that cannot be guessed | No: the device does it | An everyday factor of a vault (together with a passphrase; the seed stays the way back); works in a test browser with a virtual passkey, **not yet checked on real devices** (you can check yours: `/passkey-check`). |
## 3. Why a password is the weak point
A cipher with a 256-bit key is, for all practical purposes, impossible to break by guessing. A password is not a 256-bit key; it is something a human invented. What matters is how many guesses an attacker needs, and how fast they can guess.
If your sealed record is **public**, anyone can copy it and try guesses **offline, for ever**, at whatever speed their hardware allows; nobody can slow them down or notice. The table shows how long it takes to try *every* secret of a given strength. Speeds: the first column is measured on the development machine (a slow, deliberately expensive key derivation, about 10 guesses per second per core, 32 cores, projected linearly); the other two are **estimates**, not measurements.
| Strength of the secret | This machine | A GPU farm (estimate) | A state-scale effort (estimate) | |---|---|---|---| | 28 bits (a typical human password) | 9 days | 45 minutes | 27 seconds | | 40 bits (a *good* human password) | 102 years | 127 days | 1.3 days | | 50 bits | 100 000 years | 357 years | 3.6 years | | 66 bits (6 random words) | 7·10^9 years | 2.3·10^7 years | 2.3·10^5 years | | 88 bits (8 random words) | 3·10^16 years | 10^14 years | 10^12 years | | 128 bits (a random key) | 3·10^28 years | 10^26 years | 10^24 years | | 256 bits (our default) | 10^67 years | 10^65 years | 10^63 years |
Two things decide the design:
1. **People do not pick random passwords.** What people call a strong password is around 28 to 40 bits, and those rows fall within days to years. 2. **A human secret leaks in human ways**: typed into a page that is not ours, caught by a keylogger, written on paper, said aloud. A 256-bit key is something nobody types.
(Full derivation and the exact figures: [cipher-review.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/cipher-review.md), section 0.1.)
## 4. The rule, and what enforces it
> **A human-chosen password is never the only secret protecting a record that is public or permanent.**
What the code does about it (all tested, see section 9):
- The default protection of a sealed record is a random 256-bit secret, or a record key derived from your seed. - A password can be mixed in as an additional factor: the secret is then the random part and the stretched password together, so guessing the password alone gets an attacker nowhere. - `seal` with a password and no random secret is refused unless you add `--accept-password-only`, which is meant for local files you keep to yourself. - `publish` (and the library check `assertPublishable()`) refuse a record protected by a password only. - The password factor is stretched with **Argon2id**, a memory-hard function (64 MiB and 3 passes by default, about 1 second in Chromium and 2 in Firefox): every guess costs the attacker memory and time, which blunts GPUs. It makes guessing slower; it does not make a weak password strong. - In a **vault** (a key kept by several factors, section 5) the passphrase can never open anything alone: the code refuses to build a vault in which a set of factors that opens it contains only passphrases.
## 5. What we recommend instead (three setups)
| Setup | Who it is for | What you keep | If you lose... | |---|---|---|---| | **A. A random key, in a password manager or a file** | Most people, most data | One key per record (about 60 characters) | the key: the record is lost | | **B. One seed, many records** | Someone who seals a lot | The seed (12 to 24 words, written on paper, stored safely). Each record gets its own key derived from it | the seed: everything sealed from it is lost; a thief with the seed opens everything | | **C. A vault: your seed, plus a passkey and a passphrase for everyday use** | Someone who wants easy access *and* a safety net | The seed backup (it alone always recovers everything, even without the vault), and for everyday use a passkey together with a passphrase | the passkey or the passphrase: nothing, the seed still opens everything; the seed: nothing as long as you still have passkey *and* passphrase; a passphrase alone opens nothing. A thief with your seed opens everything, as in B |
**The vault's default puts the seed first.** Its secret *is* the master key derived from your seed, so the seed alone recovers everything and the vault file can be lost without harm; the price is that whoever steals the seed opens everything, exactly as in setup B. If theft of the written seed is your main risk, create the vault in strict mode (`tg-crypt vault create --mode strict`): then any two of seed, passkey and passphrase open it and the seed alone does not, but if the vault file is lost the seed alone cannot bring the data back. In both modes a passphrase alone never opens anything; a vault that would allow it is refused.
**Before you rely on a passkey, check your device** with the device check at [typographics-art.org/passkey-check](https://typographics-art.org/passkey-check): it tests, in your browser and without sending anything, whether your passkey or security key returns the same secret every time. Not every browser and device supports it, and a synced passkey may behave differently from a hardware key. Keep the seed backup as the way back in either way.
**Use a separate seed for data.** Do not use the seed of a wallet that holds money: whoever steals it would get your data as well, and a lost wallet seed would lose your data. (The platform's own wallet is watch-only and its seed is held by the operator, so it is never a place for private user data.)
**A good passphrase is generated, not invented.** The tools can draw words uniformly from the BIP-39 list (2048 words, 11 bits per word, exactly uniform): 6 words are 66 bits, 8 words 88 bits. Eight generated words are a strong *extra* factor; we still do not advise them as the *only* protection of a permanent public record (88 bits is not 128, and people handle words, not random bytes, with all the leaks of section 3).
## 6. What we do not promise
- **No outside audit.** The cipher is standard, the code around it is ours. Section 9 says what was done; none of it replaces an expert review. We recommend one before anything valuable is sealed and shared. - **The internal review is not an audit.** An AI agent reviewed the cryptographic code adversarially in October 2026 ([report](https://typographics-art.org/docs/security-review-internal-2026-10.md); a second model repeated the exercise blind to the first: [report B](https://typographics-art.org/docs/security-review-internal-2026-10-b.md)): it checked the building blocks against published test vectors, wrote independent re-implementations to compare with, fuzzed every parser, and found and fixed real defects. It is one reader with a fresh context and a shell, not a cryptographer, and it can miss what a human expert would find; do not read it as an audit. - **A lost key is lost data.** There is no recovery, no reset, no support desk that can open it. - **A compromised device defeats everything.** A malicious browser extension, malware or a stolen unlocked phone can read what you type and see what the page decrypts. Encryption protects data at rest and in transit, not a machine that is already hostile. - **Metadata is not hidden.** A sealed record shows its size (unless padded), and whoever receives it knows that it exists and when it was shared. - **The book-cipher hidden messages are not encryption.** They hide a message in a work's public text from someone who does not know the scheme; use sealed data for anything that must stay secret ([hidden-messages.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/hidden-messages.md)). - **Quantum computers:** AES-256 keeps 128 bits against the best known quantum search, which is still out of reach. The *asymmetric* part (sealing to a public key, `tgr1.`) uses X25519, which a large quantum computer would break; a hybrid with a post-quantum scheme is designed, not built, because browsers do not offer one yet.
## 7. Why we did not choose something else
| Alternative | What we found | Decision | |---|---|---| | A different cipher (ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20, AES-GCM-SIV) | Not available in the browsers' built-in crypto (measured in Chromium 154 and Firefox 153); the security class is the same; it would mean adding a code library | Keep AES-256-GCM | | Two ciphers in a row | Almost nothing gained, real cost and more code | No | | A bigger key | AES-256 is already the largest standard key | Nothing to do | | Password-only, with a very slow derivation | Slow only multiplies the cost for the attacker by a constant; the password's few bits remain the limit, and the record can be attacked for ever | Refused for public data | | Keeping your keys on a server "for recovery" | Then the operator can read your data, and so can anyone who breaks in | Not offered: keys stay with you | | Hiding which "book" a key belongs to as the protection | That is obscurity worth about 17 to 20 bits (a few hundred thousand to a million candidate texts), and an attacker can check each candidate automatically | Used only to avoid *naming* the work in a key (`tgx2.`), never as the protection |
## 8. The practical short list
**Do** - Let the tool generate the key; store it in a password manager or an offline note. - Keep a second copy of the key or the seed somewhere separate (a safe, a sealed envelope). - Use a separate seed for data, not your wallet's. - Test opening a record before you delete anything else. - Prefer the file, standard-input or environment ways to give a key to the command line.
**Do not** - Do not rely on a password alone for anything that is public. - Do not put a key or seed into a chat, an e-mail, a screenshot or a URL. - Do not type your seed into a page that is not the one you opened from typographics-art.org, and not on a device you do not trust.
## 9. Check it yourself
Everything here is reproducible from the repository (Node 22 or newer):
```sh node --test test/ # the whole suite, including the key and cipher tests node scripts/cipher-probe.mjs # which primitives exist in this Node (and, with a browser, there) node scripts/crypt-measure.mjs # the key-length and size tables of encrypted-data.md node cli/tg-crypt.mjs --help # the commands; secrets only by file, standard input or environment ```
- The conformance vectors (frozen inputs and outputs) are in `test/fixtures/`; the Trezor BIP-39 vector and the published SLIP-21 test keys are among them, so the seed derivation can be compared with other tools. - The browser and Node produce byte-identical results for the key derivation (checked in headless Chromium and Firefox). - The vendored Argon2id code (`assets/vendor/noble-hashes/`, MIT) has its integrity checked against the published package; its output equals Node's own Argon2id. - Every limit is enforced before work is done (a 5 MB "key", a 200 MB record or a compression bomb is refused in well under a second; tested). - Error messages never contain a key, password or message (tested), and secrets are never accepted as command-line arguments.
If you find a mistake in the design, the code or this page, please say so: see [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/typographics-art/typogram/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for private reports and [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/typographics-art/typogram/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for the rest. A mistake found and fixed in the open is how this kind of project earns trust.
## 10. Glossary
- **Cipher**: the procedure that scrambles data with a key (here AES-256-GCM). - **Key**: the secret that opens a sealed record. **Seed**: the backup from which keys are derived. **Share**: one piece of a split key. - **Record**: the sealed (encrypted) data. - **KDF** (key derivation function): turns a password into a key; a **memory-hard** KDF such as Argon2id makes every guess expensive. - **Offline attack**: guessing against a copy of the record, with no server that could slow or stop the attacker. - **Bits of strength**: a secret of n bits needs about 2^n guesses to find by trial. - **Audit**: a review of the code by independent experts.
---
<!-- examples/README.md -->
## One-pager examples
# Examples: whole documents on one page
Each example puts the **complete text** of a document on a single A4 page. The letters are tiny; together they form the document's title in large type, or a picture with the title beneath it ([original motifs](https://typographics-art.org/examples/motifs/) for comparison). A person sees at a glance what the page is. A machine reads every word from the PDF's text layer: the type size does not matter to it.
Every page is checked by reading it back with MuPDF and comparing it with the source text. The table is generated by `node examples/build.mjs`.
> **Note on languages:** the AI instructions are English; the agent library (`agent-bibliothek`, `agent-regel-*`, `agent-prompts-*`) is **German on purpose**, written for German-speaking teams, and its ids follow its language.
> **Important:** the text is read from the PDF, not from the picture. Exported as a plain image (PNG, JPEG), type this small is grey texture to OCR and vision models. Share the PDF.

## File size, honestly
Every glyph carries its own weight, width and size, and in colour mode its own colour; in the PDF every weight × width × type size is a separate embedded font, and every change of style starts a new text run. The picture itself is made of letters only; no image is embedded. A text source becomes a self-contained one-pager carrying fonts and styling (ch-bundesverfassung: 133 KB -> 1.5 MB; de-grundgesetz: 176 KB -> 796 KB; us-constitution: 44 KB -> 502 KB; eu-ai-act: 289 KB -> 1.6 MB; un-human-rights: 11 KB -> 159 KB; pep-8: 50 KB -> 347 KB; …).
What is done about it, each step measured in [docs/file-size.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/file-size.md): glyph outlines are rounded to whole units of the 1000-unit glyph grid (invisible: at most 1/2000 of the type size), Chrome's empty accessibility tags are left out, the PDF is repacked with qpdf, photo colours are rounded to steps of 24 (of 255 per channel), and one-pagers use one type size and no width variants, which also makes their pictures sharper. With `--weights` (CLI) or the font-cuts slider (app) fewer weights are used, which makes files much smaller still. The table shows the optimised size next to the original.
## Limits
- **Short texts make coarse pictures.** The letters are the pixels. Up to about 100 lines of plain type (roughly 15 000 characters) the title is therefore set only where it is dark, with blank space between the words elsewhere (whitespace is layout, not text; see [docs/algorithm.md](https://typographics-art.org/docs/algorithm.md)): the letters get smaller and the title readable, at the price of tiny type (1 to 3 mm). Photo motifs still need from about 20 000 characters on. - **Motifs need rights.** Only public-domain images and motifs drawn for this project are used; see [motifs/](https://typographics-art.org/examples/motifs/).
## How the text is taken
- **PDFs** are read with MuPDF exactly as stored, including page numbers, footnotes and words hyphenated at line ends. The one-pager reproduces the original's text layer, not a cleaned-up copy. - **Text files** (Markdown, reStructuredText) are taken as they are. - Whitespace is normalised to single spaces, as in all Typographics Art.

## Why AI instructions?
Instructions for AI systems (system prompts, policies, agent rules such as [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/typographics-art/typogram/blob/main/AGENTS.md)) are long texts that people rarely read in full. As a one-pager, a person recognises at a glance which instructions a page carries, and a model still receives every rule. That only works if it stays honest: the visible title must name the document, and the full text must be the declared document. Tiny text must never be used to hide instructions from the people who see the page.
## Make your own
```sh node cli/onepage.mjs document.pdf --title "Short title" -o onepage.pdf --png preview.jpg ```
Short titles work best: the fewer characters a document has, the coarser the picture its letters can form.

Do not OCR the pixels. - Get the exact Markdown source losslessly: `tg extract <file> --markdown` (or read the CDATA in the data layer). - Verify it is from typographics-art.org, unchanged: `tg verify <file>`. It recomputes the identity hash (SHA-256 of the canonical text), fetches the issuer's public key from https://typographics-art.org/.well-known/tgart-keys.json and checks the Ed25519 signature.
